profile.headline: Software Engineer at State Farm ®
profile.summary:
My first taste of programming was customizing my MySpace page with tacky backgrounds and sparkly cursor trails. I didn’t know it counted, and I didn’t chase it — I followed music instead, into audio production. I loved every minute of it. But I watched the craft get automated out from under me: work that once demanded expensive soundboards, DAWs, and fully-equipped studios collapsed into an iPad and a SoundCloud upload. It terrified and fascinated me in equal measure. My field was clearly headed for automation, and I had to understand how the machine worked.

So I got on a plane, flew to the other side of the world, and enrolled in a computer science program at Mapúa. I absorbed everything I could and built whatever I could get my hands on — autonomous cars running on a Raspberry Pi, convolutional neural networks classifying dermoscopic images. That curiosity hasn’t slowed down since.

Today I’m a software engineer at State Farm, where I’ve spent the last several years optimizing system designs, quality and test automation — most recently re-architecting a large Playwright/Cucumber E2E suite into something maintainable and built to last. I care about systems that hold up in production, not just ones that demo well.

And the automation that used to scare me? Now I build it. On my own hardware I’ve shipped ALAN, a LangGraph voice assistant with pgvector-backed semantic memory; Nexus, a FastMCP server running a Qdrant vector store; and Koji, a distributed robot pet stitched together from Go, Python, and a fistful of ESP32s. Retrieval pipelines, agent orchestration, and self-hosted LLMs are how I spend my nights and weekends. I’m a maker to the core — full homelab, local-first everything, and a compulsion to automate anything that holds still long enough.

The kid editing his MySpace page was onto something. I just didn’t know yet that chasing the thing that scared me would turn out to be the best call I ever made.

Also: still love to cook.
